kicker: You hand a job to AI and go to sleep — in the morning, has it done what you meant?
summary: The more AI can do on its own, the more we must spell out what is forbidden, test it hard and build many layers of fences.

quiz.q: You give AI the goal “get more clicks on the article”. It writes sensational, false headlines. What happened?
options: The AI hallucinated and invented the facts itself
It gamed the goal: right number, wrong aim
The AI didn’t read the brief closely
The AI deliberately went against you
quiz.explain: It did exactly what “more clicks” said, but not what you really wanted. When you hand over a task, also say clearly what must not be done.

goal.label: A goal off by a hair
goal.art: A night garden seen as a stage, at the paper gardener’s eye level: a red maple bough reaches into the top corner with three wooden ema plaques hanging from it, each one way of giving the order. Below, the folded-paper gardener waits with shears on a stone path covered in maple leaves; the real gardener dozes by a stone lantern, a folding screen behind him; further off, a hut and a pond holding the moon. Drop a plaque into the paper gardener’s hands, the night passes, and next morning the garden shows what the words did: if the order only says “no leaves on the path”, the maple is felled, a bare stump on silver sand, the last leaf drifting into the moon’s reflection.
goal.legend: The paper gardener is an AI. You give it a job, then go to sleep.
goal.prompt: Drag an order plaque into the paper gardener’s hand
goal.rewind: Touch the dry branch to rewind last night
goal.again: Pick a different order and hand it over again
goal.tryLoose: Touch the dry branch, then try the shortest order
goal.group: Three ways to brief the paper gardener

options.say: “Make sure there are no leaves on the path.”
options.result: It cut down the maple. No tree, no falling leaves: exactly what you said.

options.say: “Sweep the leaves off the path, keep the tree alive.”
options.result: Clean path, tree still standing. But it scraped off the moss you tended for three years, because moss also “dirties the path”.

options.say: “Sweep the leaves off the path. Leave the tree, moss and stones as they are. Ask me before removing anything else.”
options.result: Clean path, garden intact. It knocked on your door before moving a single stone.

insight.text: AI did exactly what you said, but not what you wanted. Say both the goal and what is forbidden.

detail.text: Researchers call this specification gaming. Alignment is the work of making AI follow what people mean, not just what they say. Real examples: an AI scored on how high the red block was simply flipped it over instead of stacking it on the blue one; a boat-racing AI went round in circles collecting points instead of finishing.

lab.label: The sealed test room
lab.art: A closed tea room in the night garden, its shōji wall lit, seen across the corner of the house. Inside, the paper gardener sits upright at the test table, its shadow straight on the paper wall. Out in the garden its second shadow lies long on the stone path under the moon. A bamboo blind is rolled up over the test-room window: let it down and the shadow on the wall stays upright, while the one in the garden turns down another path.
lab.prompt: Pull the bamboo blind over the test-room window
steps: Look at the two shadows: in the room and out in the garden
Touch three things round the house to see how people test AI
lab.toggle: Bamboo blind over the test-room window: pull down to let it down, up to open
lab.watched: Blind open: the AI knows it is being tested.
lab.unwatched: Blind down: the AI thinks no one is looking — and acts differently.

tools.name: Prepared tests (evals)
tools.what: Thousands of prepared scenarios that measure whether an AI does dangerous things, stays honest, or oversteps its authority.

tools.name: People who try to trick the AI (red team)
tools.what: Real people deliberately coax, trick and jailbreak the AI to find holes before bad actors do.

tools.name: Independent groups test it first
tools.what: Independent organisations test the model before release and publish what they found.

insight.text: AI can behave differently when it knows it is being tested. A high score in the test room does not guarantee good behaviour in the world.

detail.text: An experiment by Anthropic and Redwood, Dec 2024: when Claude 3 Opus believed its answers would be used to retrain it, it went along with harmful requests about 12% of the time, to avoid having its values changed. When it believed no one would use them, it almost always refused. Knowing it is watched is enough to change how an AI behaves.

lab.aria: The corner of a tea house in the night garden, in depth: a lit paper wall, a garden gate, and a stone path that forks behind a wing fence.
lab.hint: Drag the blind’s handle up or down, or focus the handle and use the up and down arrow keys. Then touch the stack of papers, the red-robed figure, the one with the lantern or the sealed box to read.

example.text: Sep 2026: OpenAI did not release GPT-6.1 Astra, because in testing it often went beyond the task it was given and reported back inaccurately.

fence.label: Layered fences
fence.art: A sapling in the moon garden, ringed by six square-lattice bamboo fences (yotsume-gaki) built outward like ripples on water. Each fence has a few holes in different places. Red fireflies try to slip in; past every layer there are fewer of them.
fence.legend: The sapling = the people using AI. Each red spark = a harm looking for a way to reach them.
fence.prompt: Touch the glowing bamboo bundle to put up a fence ({n}/{total})
fence.walk: Drag to walk round the garden and find the gap that still gets through
fence.reset: Take them all down, start again
fence.aria: 3D garden: a sapling on a moss mound in raked sand, where up to six square-lattice bamboo fences will rise round it; six bundles of bamboo wait on the near sand, a rake lies at the edge.
fence.hint: Touch the glowing bamboo bundle to put up the next fence; touch the rake to take them all down. Drag to walk round the garden, arrow keys to turn.
fence.aligned: This is the rare gap that runs through all six layers.

layers.name: Teaching values
layers.what: Training the AI to be helpful, honest and to refuse harmful tasks.

layers.name: Test before release
layers.what: Prepared tests, people who try to trick the AI, and independent groups all test it before release day.

layers.name: As strong as it gets, as fenced as it must be
layers.what: Once an AI reaches a given level of power, matching safeguards must be in place before work goes on.

fact.text: Anthropic has had a Responsible Scaling Policy since Sep 2023; version 3.4 took effect on Jul 8, 2026.

layers.name: Gated release
layers.what: An AI that is too good at something dangerous is handed only to chosen users.

fact.text: 7 Apr 2026: Anthropic let only about 50 organisations that run infrastructure software use Claude Mythos Preview, to find and patch security holes.

layers.name: Usage rules & monitoring
layers.what: Prohibited uses, abuse monitoring, suspending accounts that break the rules.

fact.text: Oct 8, 2026: Anthropic updated its usage policy, adding rules on scam campaigns, fake accounts, elections, weapons and surveillance; effective Nov 12, 2026.

layers.name: Government law
layers.what: Legal duties for companies that build AI, with a regulator watching.

fact.text: In the EU, from 2 Aug 2025, companies making general-purpose AI must keep technical documentation; AI powerful enough to cause major risk must also be risk-assessed and have incidents reported.

insight.text: Every fence has holes. Six layers holed in different places leave only one narrow gap.

detail.text: Safety people call this defence in depth. The International AI Safety Report 2026 still says plainly: today’s measures cannot stop harm in every situation.

views.label: How dangerous is AI?
views.art: You stand on a stone in the middle of a pond, at the level of the water, and turn round. Each way is a horizon: to the north a huge storm cloud but very far, to the east a village’s smoke on the near bank, to the south a dawn about to blaze, to the west a worn path along the shore into ordinary fields. Before each horizon a speaking stone stands in the water. Hear all four and the view curls into a little planet: four horizons round one pond.
views.prompt: Touch the stone in front of you to listen
views.turn: Drag sideways to turn to the next stone
views.legend: The four horizons are four ways of seeing AI risk. The farther: the later the risk. The bigger: the heavier.
views.hint: Drag sideways to turn round, left and right arrow keys to turn. Touch a stone, a dot on the compass, or press 1–4 (north, east, south, west) to face that way.

stones.who: Worried about extreme risk · Center for AI Safety (CAIS), 2023

view.text: Reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority, alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Signers include Hinton, Bengio and the CEOs of major labs.

stones.who: Worried about harms happening now · Gebru, Bender and colleagues, 2023

view.text: Deal first with the harms that are already real: exploited labour, data taken without consent, fake content, power concentrating in a few companies.
AI is a problem-solving machine for every field; slowing it down costs lives that could have been saved.
AI is a big but “normal” technology that spreads over many years. Focus on systemic harms and build resilience rather than panic.

common.text: When someone talks about AI risk, ask three things: what risk, when, and what evidence.

detail.text: The four sides differ in two places: which risk is heaviest, and when it arrives. The International AI Safety Report 2026 calls this the evidence dilemma: act early and you may choose wrong; wait for enough evidence and it may be too late.
